propositions.text: Claimant is a 42-year-old male from Georgia claiming fear of persecution on religious grounds and risk of torture or cruel treatment.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX is a 42-year-old male and a national of Georgia. He claims to have a well-founded fear of persecution on the grounds of religion. He also claims to be a person in danger of torture and a person who faces a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant is a 42-year-old Georgian male claiming religious persecution and risk of torture or cruel treatment, as stated by the court.

propositions.text: The IRB finds the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) determines that the claimant is neither a "Convention refugee" nor a "person in need of protection."

paragraphs.summary: The IRB decides the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection, as found by the court.

propositions.text: Claimant's identity established by original Georgian passport and testimony on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: The identity of the claimant was established to the tribunal's satisfaction by his original Georgian passport. Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC)1 submitted photocopies of the claimant's passport. Based on the passport and the testimony of the claimant, the tribunal is satisfied that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant has established his identity.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant's identity established by his original Georgian passport and testimony on a balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges he is Christian in common-law partnership with Muslim woman whose family opposed marriage unless he converted to Islam.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that he is Christian and is in a common-law partnership (at times referring to her as his wife) with XXXX XXXX, a Muslim girl, whom he met in 2001. They wanted to marry but her parents opposed the marriage unless the claimant became a Muslim.

propositions.text: In-laws objected to son being registered under claimant's name unless he converted to Islam; claimant promised but did not convert.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, his in-laws objected to the claimant registering his son, born in 2002, under his name unless he agreed to convert to Islam. The claimant promised that he would convert and registered his son under his name. However, he did not convert.

propositions.text: In-laws did not allow claimant and son to attend church.
propositions.quote: He alleges that her family did not allow him and his son to go to church.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges religious persecution by his Muslim in-laws opposing marriage and church attendance, as he states.

propositions.text: Claimant and family moved to Tbilisi in 2009; claimant worked and attended church without issue initially.
propositions.quote: On September 1, 2009, the claimant, his wife, and son moved from XXXX to Tbilisi. The claimant stated that everything went smoothly. His son was going to school; the claimant was working at the porcelain company and attending a Christian Orthodox Church.

propositions.text: Father-in-law and brother-in-law demanded claimant convert to Islam; claimant refused and moved family to parents' home in 2010 for protection.
propositions.quote: The claimant wrote in his narrative that his father-in-law and brother-in-law came to his home in Tbilisi and once again demanded that he convert to the Muslim faith. He told them that he would not obey, and on June 15, 2010, moved his family to his parents' home in Gurjaani to help protect his family from pressure for him to convert to Islam.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant says he initially lived peacefully in Tbilisi but moved to parents' home in 2010 after in-laws pressured him to convert to Islam.

propositions.text: Claimant and cousin borrowed $30,000 to open business; merchandise seized by Revenue of Georgia causing financial loss.
propositions.quote: The company where the claimant worked closed and he and his cousin, XXXX XXXX, borrowed $30,000 from XXXX XXXX to open a business. The moving company which they used to import clothing from Turkey was sequestered by Revenue of Georgia and the claimant and his cousin lost their money since their merchandise could not be delivered.

propositions.text: Father-in-law colluded with lender to harass claimant; in-laws physically assaulted claimant causing unconsciousness and hospitalization.
propositions.quote: His father-in-law told the lender that the claimant and his cousin could not repay the monies. His father-in-law colluded with the lender, XXXX XXXX, to make the claimant's life a nightmare. The claimant's in-laws went to the claimant's home, cursed at him, and beat him with a stick and belt until he was unconscious. The claimant came to in the hospital.

propositions.text: Claimant's father promised to file police complaint; police refused to act citing domestic violence.
propositions.quote: His father was there and said that he would file a complaint with the police. The claimant alleges that XXXX uncle was behind the police, who refused to do anything about the incident citing that it was domestic violence.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges financial loss, collusion by father-in-law and lender, and physical assaults by in-laws with police inaction.

propositions.text: Claimant was kidnapped once and beaten multiple times; after last incident in February 2011, family decided he should leave Georgia.
propositions.quote: The claimant was kidnapped once and beaten again on several other occasions. After the last incident on February XXXX, 2011, the claimant and his family decided that he should leave Georgia.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant states he was kidnapped and beaten multiple times, prompting family decision to leave Georgia after February 2011 incident.

propositions.text: Claimant left Georgia April 2011, stayed in France April 2011-August 2012, then arrived in Canada August 2012.
propositions.quote: He left Georgia on April XXXX, 2011 to go stay with a friend in Canada. He went to France and stayed there from April XXXX, 2011 until August XXXX, 2012. He then left France on August XXXX, 2012. He arrived in Canada on August XXXX, 2012.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant left Georgia in April 2011, stayed in France until August 2012, then arrived in Canada, as he states.

propositions.text: Tribunal found claimant's testimony inconsistent, vague, evasive, contradictory, and confusing.
propositions.quote: The tribunal had difficulty in getting consistent testimony from the claimant. His answers were vague, evasive, contradictory, and confusing.

propositions.text: Tribunal considered both claimant's narratives and Port of Entry interview notes.
propositions.quote: The tribunal did take into account both of the claimant's narratives. The first was part of his PIF, received at the IRB on September 17, 2012, and the second received on July 24, 2018.2 The tribunal also referred to the Port of Entry (POE) interview notes.3

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal found the claimant's testimony inconsistent and considered both narratives and POE interview notes.

propositions.text: Claim for refugee protection hinges on two factors.
propositions.quote: The claim for refugee protection which the claimant presented hinges on two factors.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the refugee claim depends on two factors.

propositions.text: First factor: problems with in-laws due to claimant's Christianity and partner's Muslim faith.
propositions.quote: The first factor is his problems with his in-laws stemming from him being a Christian and his common-law partner being Muslim.

propositions.text: Second factor: $30,000 debt with cousin, with in-laws colluding with lender to harass claimant.
propositions.quote: The second is that he and his cousin have a debt of $30,000, which he has not repaid, and as a result of which his in-laws are colluding with the lender to make the claimant's life a nightmare.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies two claim factors: religious problems with in-laws and a $30,000 debt with lender collusion.

propositions.text: Tribunal does not believe either claim for specified reasons.
propositions.quote: The tribunal does not believe either one of these claims for the following reasons. Religion

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal disbelieves both claims for reasons to follow, starting with religion.

propositions.text: CBSA agent questioned claimant with Russian interpreter about reasons for leaving Georgia.
propositions.quote: The CBSA agent questioned the claimant with a Russian interpreter, as requested by the claimant.

propositions.text: Claimant said problems were with 'criminal authorities' described vaguely as 'bossy people' who can kill citizens.
propositions.quote: The claimant responded that he was having problems with the "criminal authorities." When asked what he meant by criminal authorities, the claimant responded, "people who are the bossy people." The claimant responded, "Criminal authority are the people who control the situation."

propositions.text: Agent told claimant he was being intentionally vague and reminded him of legal obligation to answer.
propositions.quote: The agent told the claimant that he was being intentionally vague. The agent had to remind the claimant that he was required by law to answer his questions.

propositions.text: Claimant repeated vague answers about criminal authorities and large unpaid loan.
propositions.quote: The claimant said that he was answering all of the agent's questions and again gave, in the tribunal's view, a vague answer: "Criminal authorities are those people who can go to any citizen and just kill them." Eventually, he said that he borrowed a large amount of money and could not repay it.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts CBSA questioning where claimant gave vague answers about criminal authorities and unpaid loan.

propositions.text: Claimant never mentioned religion or in-laws forcing conversion during CBSA questioning despite being asked about persecution.
propositions.quote: The claimant never mentioned religion, even though he was asked why he feared persecution in Georgia. He did say that he was married. It was said several different ways that the persecution was from the criminal authorities. He never mentioned religion or his in-laws forcing him to convert or him being Christian and his wife being Muslim.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant never mentioned religious persecution or in-laws forcing conversion during CBSA questioning.

propositions.text: Claimant explained omission of religious persecution at border was to be brief and would explain later.
propositions.quote: Confronted with why he did not mention religious persecution, he responded that it was to be brief and that he would tell it later in his story.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant argues he omitted religious persecution at border to be brief and planned to explain later.

propositions.text: Tribunal concludes claimant fabricated religious persecution story due to omission at border and inconsistent explanation.
propositions.quote: The tribunal concluded that the claimant fabricated the story about the gravity of his religious problems, if in fact they exist, as he did not state it to the CBSA as the reason for his being persecuted.

propositions.text: Claimant's explanation to be brief is negated by CBSA evidence showing he was asked to explain.
propositions.quote: His explanation that he was told to be brief is negated by the CBSA factual evidence when to the contrary, he was asked to explain.

propositions.text: If religious persecution was a reason for leaving Georgia, claimant would have mentioned it at border; omission undermines credibility.
propositions.quote: If religious persecution is in fact one of the two reasons that the claimant left Georgia, the tribunal does not find it credible that the claimant would not mention it at the border.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds claimant fabricated religious persecution claim due to omission at border and inconsistent explanation, undermining credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant alleges $30,000 loan borrowed with cousin, unable to repay; father-in-law told lender claimant would not repay, leading to abuse and police inaction.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that he and his cousin borrowed money and were not able to repay it. The claimant wrote in his narratives that his cousin decided to sell his house but they needed time. The loan was taken out in the second half of 2010. Allegedly, his father-in-law told the lender on October 20, 2010, that he, the claimant, was not going to repay the loan. As a result, he was verbally abused and beaten by his in-laws and other persons that were in collusion with the lender. When one of the beatings landed the claimant in the hospital, his father made a complaint to the police, who refused to deal with the problem, saying that it was domestic violence.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges a $30,000 loan with cousin, father-in-law told lender claimant wouldn't repay, causing abuse and police refusal to act.

propositions.text: Claimant said cousin would sell house to repay loan; cousin provided statement confirming intent to sell house and repay loan.
propositions.quote: The claimant said that he and his cousin borrowed $30,000 that they could not repay. Then he said that his cousin would sell his house and repay the loan but it would take time. The claimant's cousin provided a statement4 confirming that he had a desire to sell his house and repay the loan.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant states cousin would sell house to repay loan, supported by cousin's statement confirming intent.

propositions.text: Claimant told CBSA problems were with criminal authorities and unpaid loan; cousin's plan to repay loan removes lender's reason to pursue claimant.
propositions.quote: The tribunal cannot ignore what the claimant said to the agent at the CBSA. He kept insisting that he was having problems with the criminal authorities, bossy people, those people that can go to any citizen and just kill them. Later, he mentions a loan that he could not repay. Giving the claimant the benefit of the doubt that there was a loan taken out by him and his cousin, his cousin said that he was going to sell his house to repay the loan. Once the debt is gone, the lender would have no reason to pursue the claimant.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal notes claimant told CBSA about criminal authorities and unpaid loan; cousin's repayment plan negates lender's motive to pursue claimant.

propositions.text: Tribunal accepts medical records of injuries but doubts injuries resulted from in-laws' religious pressure due to inconsistent claimant accounts.
propositions.quote: The claimant submitted a copious amount of letters from Georgia. The tribunal does not question the medical records as to the injuries he sustained. However, the tribunal does not believe that he sustained these injuries because of his in-laws wanting him to convert to Islam for reasons previously discussed.

propositions.text: Claimant's explanations of how injuries occurred are questionable and inconsistent with CBSA statements.
propositions.quote: How and why he sustained the injuries is questionable since he told the CBSA it was the criminal authorities that were after him and he told the tribunal that it was the person who lent him the money, his father-in-law, and his brother-in law.

propositions.text: Tribunal accepts medical conditions as true but gives no probative value to claimant's account of injury causes due to family dispute or general beating.
propositions.quote: The tribunal does not question the veracity of the medical conditions in the reports.5 However, the tribunal gives no probative value as to how the injuries occurred since it is the claimant that told the doctor what happened and the details are either family dispute or general account of being beaten.

propositions.text: Death certificate of claimant's father is not in question.
propositions.quote: The death certificate of his father6 is also not in question.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal accepts medical records but doubts injuries resulted from religious pressure, finds claimant's injury accounts inconsistent, and accepts father's death certificate.

propositions.text: There is the issue of the claimant's travel history and refugee protection claims in France.
propositions.quote: There is also the issue of travel. The claimant left Georgia and went to stay in Paris, France for approximately fifteen months, according to question 11 in his PIF.

propositions.text: The claimant stayed in Paris for about fifteen months and did not seek refugee protection there, waiting for papers to come to Canada.
propositions.quote: When questioned as to whether he asked for refugee protection in France and what he did in France, he said that he did not ask for refugee protection, that he was waiting for papers to come to Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the claimant stayed in Paris for about fifteen months and did not seek refugee protection there, waiting for Canadian papers.

propositions.text: Claimant is not required to seek refugee protection at first opportunity but a long stay in a signatory country raises expectation to seek protection.
propositions.quote: Although the claimant is not required to seek refugee protection at the first opportunity, the claimant was in France for over one year. It was not a brief stopover. France is a signatory of the Geneva Convention.

propositions.text: The claimant alleges he feared for his life and thus did not seek protection in France.
propositions.quote: The claimant alleges that he feared for his life.

propositions.text: It is not unreasonable for the tribunal to expect the claimant to seek protection in France given the circumstances.
propositions.quote: It is not unreasonable for the tribunal to expect that he would seek protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court states claimant was not required to seek protection immediately but should have in France; claimant alleges fear for life.

propositions.text: The tribunal draws a negative inference about the claimant's story due to his failure to seek protection in France.
propositions.quote: The tribunal draws a negative inference and this further puts into question the claimant's story.

propositions.text: The tribunal believes the claimant fabricated his story, which was inconsistent with CBSA and PIF narratives.
propositions.quote: The tribunal believes that the claimant wanted to come to Canada and fabricated his story, which was inconsistent from the CBSA and the narratives in his PIF.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds the claimant fabricated his story and draws a negative inference from inconsistencies and failure to seek protection in France.

propositions.text: Due to general lack of credibility, the tribunal does not believe other incidents claimed by the claimant occurred.
propositions.quote: Given the general lack of credibility of the claimant, the tribunal does not believe that the other incidents occurred.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal does not believe other incidents claimed due to claimant's general lack of credibility.

propositions.text: The tribunal finds the claimant does not face a serious risk of persecution if returned to Georgia due to lack of credibility.
propositions.quote: Given the finding that the claimant's story is not credible, the tribunal believes that the claimant does not face a serious risk of persecution should he return to Georgia.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds claimant does not face serious persecution risk in Georgia due to lack of credibility.

propositions.text: The tribunal concludes claimant is not credible and cannot establish serious risk of persecution for religion.
propositions.quote: The tribunal, having come to the conclusion that the claimant is not credible and not able to establish that there is a serious possibility that he would be persecuted for reason of religion,

propositions.text: The tribunal analyzed all evidence and determined claimant faces no risk to life, cruel treatment, or need for protection under IRPA.
propositions.quote: turned to look at all the evidence submitted to determine if the claimant is a person in need of protection. The tribunal analyzed the claim from the perspective of a person in need of protection and has determined that the claimant faces neither a risk to life nor a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment nor is he a person in need of protection as defined in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal finds claimant not credible and not at risk of persecution or cruel treatment, thus not in need of protection under IRPA.

propositions.text: The tribunal finds claimant has not discharged his burden of proof after considering all evidence.
propositions.quote: After having considered all testimonies, both written and oral, the tribunal finds that the claimant has not discharged his burden of proof.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal concludes claimant failed to discharge burden of proof after considering all evidence.

propositions.text: The tribunal determines claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection under IRPA.
propositions.quote: Based upon the above analysis, the tribunal determines that XXXX XXXXXXXX is neither a "Convention refugee" as defined in section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act nor a "person in need of protection" as defined in section 97(1) of that law.

paragraphs.summary: The tribunal determines claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection under IRPA.
